title: Reversals and Hidden Assumptions
summary: Learn to spot invalid reversals, hidden assumptions and other common reasoning traps in Statements and Conclusions questions.
learningObjectives: Recognize when a statement has been reversed incorrectly
Distinguish valid conversions from invalid reversals
Identify hidden assumptions in proposed conclusions
Avoid conclusions that add unstated information

contentBlocks.content: Many incorrect conclusions look convincing because they reverse the direction of a statement or quietly add information that was never given. Strong logical reasoning requires you to notice these hidden changes.

contentBlocks.title: Invalid reversal
contentBlocks.content: Statement: All engineers are graduates. Conclusion: All graduates are engineers. This does not follow. The original statement places engineers inside the graduate group, but the graduate group may contain many other people.

contentBlocks.title: What can be safely reversed?
contentBlocks.content: 'Some A are B' can be read as 'Some B are A' because the same shared members belong to both groups. 'No A are B' can be read as 'No B are A' because the groups do not overlap. But 'All A are B' cannot normally be reversed.

contentBlocks.title: Adding an unstated fact
contentBlocks.content: Statement: Some employees received bonuses. Conclusion: The highest-performing employees received bonuses. The conclusion adds a performance condition that the statement never mentions.

contentBlocks.title: Do not assume 'only'
contentBlocks.content: Statement: All doctors in this clinic wear white coats. This does not mean that only doctors wear white coats. Nurses, technicians or other people may also wear them.

contentBlocks.title: Do not add causes or reasons
contentBlocks.content: A statement may tell you that two facts are connected without explaining why. Do not invent a cause, motive or reason unless the statement actually provides one.

contentBlocks.title: Trap-check method
items: Compare the direction of the conclusion with the original statement.
Check whether the conclusion adds words such as only, always, best, first or most.
Look for new causes, reasons or conditions.
Check whether personal knowledge has been added.
Accept only what the statements themselves guarantee.

contentBlocks.title: Check your understanding
contentBlocks.content: Statement: Some lawyers are lecturers. Conclusion: Some lecturers are lawyers. This follows because the same people who are both lawyers and lecturers can be described from either direction.

contentBlocks.title: Lesson summary
contentBlocks.content: Invalid conclusions often reverse an all statement or introduce information that was never given. Some and no statements can be converted safely, but all statements generally cannot.

contentBlocks.title: Key takeaways
items: All A are B does not mean all B are A.
Some A are B means some B are A.
No A are B means no B are A.
Never add 'only' unless the statement provides it.
Never add causes, motives or facts that are not stated.
